items.title: Create Time Dependent Dimension with Multiple Time Dependent Sources
items.author: vineet_gupta3
items.text: SAP Datasphere offers clears guidance on how to model a dimension view where attributes are time dependent. It gets complicated when you have attributes from multiple sources, each with independent time intervals. One approach is to have independent time dependent views for each source and then daisy chain them with associations to achieve the final dimension view. This blog provides an alternate approach using sql view to merge time intervals for each source and still maintain correct values for all attributes.

items.title: Enterprise Solution Development with SAP Joule Studio
items.author: hkaur
items.text: Introduction Joule Studio is SAP's AI-first development environment that enables organisations to build and deploy enterprise-grade agents, workflows, and applications simply by describing what they want to achieve. This blog walks through its key capabilities, how it works, and the value it brings to businesses running on SAP. At its core, Joule Studio provides low-code capabilities to build and operate AI agents, automated workflows, and applications all governed by the enterprise-grade controls and deep business understanding that SAP systems demand. The platform is accessible through two complementary paths: Joule Studio Web UI A conversational, browser-based experience that allows business users and citizen developers to describe what they want in plain language and watch the platform translate that description into a working solution. Joule Studio CLI A command-line interface designed for professional developers who prefer working within their local IDE while following the same intent-based methodology. Both paths share the same underlying philosophy: intent-based development, which anchors every solution firmly in real business objectives rather than technical abstractions. The Intent-Based Development Model The most distinctive characteristic of Joule Studio is its intent-based development model. Rather than asking developers to begin with architecture diagrams, API catalogues, or data models, Joule Studio starts with a simple question: What outcome do you need? This approach is captured in a structured, six-step process. While the steps represent a logical progression, they are deliberately non-linear. Teams can revisit earlier stages after reviewing generated artefacts, refine their intent once they see the automatically produced specification, or loop back to adjust requirements after testing. Step 1: Intent The journey begins when a user describes their business challenge and the solution they envision in natural language. After the intent is defined, Joule Studio initiates a solution discovery process, consulting multiple SAP knowledge sources to design an architecturally sound solution within the constraints of the customer's specific SAP landscape. Users who want to move quickly can use the Quick Create option to bypass clarifying questions and proceed directly to solution generation. Step 2: Requirements Once the intent has been validated and enriched through discovery, all gathered information is synthesized into a formal Product Requirements Document (PRD). This document contains structured user personas, requirements expressed as user stories, explicit scope boundaries, and a high-level architectural overview. Step 3: Specification The next phase is specification phase, generating an implementation blueprint. This blueprint encompasses architecture decisions, API references, data models, and a prioritised task list. Joule Studio automatically discovers relevant SAP APIs from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, sparing developers from the time-consuming task of searching through hundreds of available APIs manually. Step 4: Solution This is where code becomes reality. Based on the approved specification, Joule Studio generates production-ready agents, automations, and applications precisely tailored to the customer's SAP landscape. These are not generic templates but they are architecture-aware artefacts that reflect the systems, deployment models, and integration patterns already in place. Step 5: Testing Before anything reaches production, the solution is deployed to an isolated sandbox environment for thorough validation. The testing step allows developers and business users to interact with the solution, verify that it meets stated requirements and success criteria defined during PRD phase, and confirm that it behaves correctly against real data and system interactions. Step 6: Deployment The final step sees the solution transition from development to production. It is worth noting that the developer's responsibility at this stage is to validate the solution in development. Solution Discovery Joule Studio consults multiple intelligence sources before proposing any solution architecture. SAP LeanIX : Enterprise Landscape Understanding SAP LeanIX provides context about the customer's specific SAP environment: which systems are deployed and how the organisation is structured. This contextual grounding ensures that proposed solutions actually work within the customer's real landscape. SAP Knowledge Graph : API Discovery and Architecture Mapping The SAP Knowledge Graph maps business needs to SAP's Reference Business Architecture. It identifies relevant APIs with their full specifications and authentication requirements, and it performs a fit-gap analysis that determines which capabilities already exist in standard SAP offerings versus which aspects require custom development. SAP Domain Models : Best Practices and Intelligence SAP Domain Models guide the solution towards proven architecture patterns, appropriate security and compliance controls, and established SAP design patterns. SAP Signavio: Process Insights SAP Signavio supplies process intelligence that give insights into how business processes are actually running which in turn helps to ground the proposed solution in real, observed process behaviour within the organization. Accessing Joule Studio Via Joule Work: The primary access point for most users is through Joule Work , SAP's intelligent workspace UI. Users navigate to Joule Studio by selecting Develop from the main navigation bar within Joule Work. The integration is intentional. Because Joule Work already understands the user's role, context, and connected systems, the transition into development mode is seamless. Via the CLI: For professional developers, the CLI provides a code-first path that integrates with any modern IDE. Developers can follow the same intent-based process — describing their intent in a configuration file, generating specifications and the final solution. Solution Types in Joule Studio Joule Studio supports distinct types of solutions( rapidly evolving), each addressing different automation and intelligence scenarios. Agents: Agents are the centrepiece capability of Joule Studio. An agent understands natural language, accesses SAP data, and executes tasks through conversation. What an Agent Can Do : A Joule Studio agent possesses several core capabilities: Natural language comprehension — Users ask questions or give commands in plain language, without needing to frame requests in technical terms. SAP system connectivity — The agent connects to SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools . This provides a secure, governed connection to backend data. Tool execution — Agents can invoke specific actions such as querying financial data, analysing operational trends, or generating insights from business records. Contextual decision-making — The agent determines which APIs to call based on the context of a conversation, without the user needing to specify technical details. Agent-to-agent communication — Through the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol, agents can discover and invoke other agents, enabling orchestrated multi-agent workflows that tackle complex, multi-domain tasks. Agent Skills : Within the agent architecture, "skills" represent discrete capabilities. A skill might be retrieving invoice data from SAP, calculating a financial impact across a date range, or summarising supplier performance across a quarter. Skills define the scope of agent action and are exposed to Joule's routing engine. SAP System Connectivity and Security : Agents access SAP backends through a secure, governed gateway — the Agent Gateway which serves as the single controlled connection point between agents and SAP systems. Automatic Discovery Through Joule : Once deployed, an agent becomes automatically discoverable through Joule. When a user asks a question that falls within the agent's declared area of responsibility, Joule routes that request to the agent transparently. SAP Managed n8n Workflows: Structured Process Automation: Joule Studio provides SAP Managed n8n Workflows — a workflow automation tool that orchestrates multi-step business processes within SAP's governed environment. A workflow is composed of nodes — building blocks that retrieve, process, transform, or transmit data. Nodes are connected sequentially, with each node consuming the output of its predecessor. The workflow begins with a trigger that determines when and how the automation starts, followed by one or more processing nodes. What Workflows Enable The range of automation scenarios addressable through SAP Managed n8n is broad: Approval automation: Route documents, invoices, or procurement requests through multi-level approval chains. Deliver approval tasks directly to SAP Task Center for streamlined action. Business Rules and Conditional Branching : Workflows support conditional logic described in natural language. For instance: if an invoice amount is below a specified threshold, approve it automatically; if it exceeds that threshold, route it to a manager for review. Joule Studio translates the plain language description into the corresponding workflow branching logic, eliminating the need for manual configuration. Workflow Node Architecture : Nodes are the operational units of a workflow. In Joule Studio, two categories of nodes are available: Standard n8n Nodes, SAP-Specific Nodes that have Pre built SAP Connectors. Agent Extensions : Dynamic Customisation at Runtime : Beyond standalone agents and automated workflows, Joule Studio introduces a third solution type: Agent Extensions. These provide capailities to customise and extend existing agent capabilities dynamically at runtime, without requiring modification of the base agent itself. Agent Extensions are valuable in scenarios where users can Inject organisation-specific logic or policy constraints into an agent's behaviour without altering its core architecture. Creating a Solution The Web UI Walkthrough : For users working through the Web UI, creating a solution follows a straightforward process: 1. Open Joule Work and navigate to the Develop section from the main navigation bar. 2. Select the solution type — choose from an Agent tile, an n8n Workflow tile, or an Agent Extension tile, or describe the challenge in the chat window and let Joule Studio recommend the appropriate type. 3. Provide the solution details — enter a name for the solution and an intent statement that describes the goal. For agent extensions, use the Agent Catalog to select the target agent. 4. Choose the creation mode — either enable Quick Create to proceed immediately without clarifying questions, or use the guided approach. 5. Select Create — Joule Studio initiates the discovery and generation process. Solution Artefacts, Git Integration, and Collaboration Solution Artefacts: Each solution produced by Joule Studio consists of one or more solution artefacts — discrete components that can be configured, tested, and deployed independently. This granularity supports modular development patterns and enables teams to stage the rollout of complex multi-component solutions. Connecting to Git : Joule Studio integrates with Git repositories, enabling teams to manage their generated code using standard version control practices. This Git connectivity is essential for the deployment handoff process, as the production deployment pipeline is triggered from the GitHub repository to which the developer pushes the validated solution. Solution Collaboration : Enterprise solutions are rarely the work of a single individual. Joule Studio's collaboration feature allows solution owners to share access with colleagues, enabling joint development within the same solution context. As the owner, you control precisely who can access the solution and what level of involvement each collaborator is permitted — aligning with standard ent

items.title: Relembre a palestra: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2, a evolução do CRM da SAP #SITCWB2026
items.author: AdrianoCWB
items.text:
No dia 7 de novembro, no Auditório Gregor Mendel da PUCPR, Clóvis Müller, Consultor Funcional SAP Sales & Service Cloud, com 12 anos de experiência em CRM, apresentou no SAP Inside Track Curitiba 2026 a palestra "Conheça o SAP Sales & Service Cloud Versão 2: A Evolução do CRM da SAP". 
 Sobre a palestra 
 Clóvis apresentou a Versão 2 do SAP Sales & Service Cloud, dentro da suíte SAP Customer Experience. Todas as soluções conectam-se pelo SAP BTP, com integrações pré-configuradas e fluxo de dados em tempo real. 
 A evolução do SAP CRM 
 Até 2013: SAP CRM, on-premise (o mais usado foi o 7.0). 
 2013 a 2016: SAP Hybris, após a compra da Hybris. 
 2018: SAP C/4HANA. 
 2020: SAP Sales & Service Cloud, conhecido como C4C. 
 2023: SAP Sales & Service Cloud Versão 2, plataforma cloud-native baseada em microsserviços e APIs, com IA. Segundo a palestra, não é só uma atualização, é uma reestruturação completa. 
 O que mostrou na prática 
 Sales Cloud: visão 360° do cliente, ciclo de vendas do lead ao pedido, gestão de oportunidades, da oportunidade à cotação, dashboards e uso pelo celular. 
 Service Cloud: atendimento multicanal (chat, e-mail, telefone, WhatsApp), identificação automática do cliente, base de conhecimento, SLAs e criação de solicitações. 
 Recursos de IA: pontuação de leads, resumo da conta e análise de sentimento. 
 Para aprender mais 
 A palestra indicou o SAP Help Portal e o SAP Learning para documentação e treinamentos. 
 Sobre o palestrante 
 Clóvis Müller, consultor SAP Sales Cloud e Service Cloud, certificado SAP nas versões 1 e 2 das duas soluções.

 Currently, we have uploaded a single PEM file containing the complete certificate chain , consisting of: 
 Root CA Certificate: Remains unchanged. 
 Intermediate CA Certificate: Remains unchanged. 
 Leaf (Server) Certificate: Automatically rotates approximately every 30 days. 
 Since the MQTT broker's leaf certificate is periodically renewed, we would like clarification on the following: 

 Certificate Rotation: When the MQTT broker's leaf certificate rotates, do we need to upload the updated PEM file containing the complete certificate chain again in SAP DM's Manage Message Brokers application? 

 CA-Based Trust: If the Root and Intermediate CA certificates remain unchanged, will SAP DM Production Connector automatically trust the renewed leaf certificate without requiring any manual certificate update?

 Recommended Configuration: Can we configure only the Root and Intermediate CA certificates in the PEM file to avoid updating the certificate configuration whenever the leaf certificate rotates? 

 Connectivity Impact: Does leaf certificate rotation require any configuration redeployment or Production Connector restart to maintain MQTT connectivity? Our objective is to ensure uninterrupted MQTT connectivity without manually updating the certificate configuration every 30 days. Please help us with the right approach to resolve this. items.title: Asset Accounting- Depreciation calculation change from Gross to Net
items.author: nag_7589
items.text:
Hello Experts, 
 We have two company codes using SAP Asset Accounting: 
 GR01 (Germany) – Asset Accounting implemented in 1996 
 C001 (Canada) – Asset Accounting implemented in 2025 
 We noticed that depreciation postings are handled differently between the two company codes. 
 1. Germany (GR01) – Gross Method 
 Asset acquisition: 
 Dr Technical Equipment (Asset G/L 100000) = 100,000 
 Cr Vendor 
 Monthly depreciation posting: 
 Dr Depreciation Expense (G/L 7000 - Deduction for wear and tear) 
 Cr Asset Reconciliation Account (G/L 100000) 
 As a result, depreciation is posted directly against the asset account. 
 2. Canada (C001) – Net Method 
 Asset acquisition: 
 Dr Technical Equipment (Asset G/L 100000) = 100,000 
 Cr Vendor 
 Monthly depreciation posting: 
 Dr Depreciation Expense (G/L 7000 - Deduction for wear and tear) 
 Cr Accumulated Depreciation (G/L 200000) 
 In this case, the asset acquisition cost remains unchanged and depreciation is accumulated on a separate accumulated depreciation account. 
 Requirement 
 We would like to understand how to change the German company code from the current gross posting method to the net posting method , similar to the Canadian setup. 
 Questions 
 Which SAP Asset Accounting configuration determines whether depreciation is posted using the gross or net method? 
 Is this controlled by: 
 Depreciation Area settings? 
 Account Determination (AO90)? 
 Transaction types? 
 Another configuration object? 
 What is the recommended procedure to switch an existing company code from gross to net depreciation posting? 
 What impact would this change have on: 
 Existing fixed assets 
 Accumulated depreciation values 
 Historical depreciation postings 
 Financial statements / balance sheet reporting 
 Has anyone performed such a conversion in a productive system, and are there any specific risks or SAP notes that should be considered? 
 Any guidance or best practices would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thank you in advance.

items.title: AI Is Changing the First Job: Why Youth Employment Belongs on Every Business Agenda
items.author: Maximilian Herrmann
items.text:
This summer, researchers at Stanford used U.S. payroll data to see where AI is already changing employment. 
 Explore how SAP turns bold ideas into measurable change for people and planet 

 Learn more 

 Among 22- to 25-year-olds, employment in the jobs most exposed to AI has fallen 19% behind employment in less-exposed jobs. Experienced workers show no such gap.* The change is happening where careers start. 

 Young people were already struggling to find work before AI arrived. According to the International Labor Organization, 257 million young people are not in employment, education, or training—9 million more than in 2023. 

 Over the next decade, around 1.2 billion young people in emerging economies will reach working age, while only about 420 million jobs are expected to be created there, according to the World Bank Group. 

 Why this is a business question 

 Entry-level jobs are where people learn how work actually gets done and build their first professional networks. Over time, they become the experienced staff on which companies rely. If AI takes over many of the tasks that used to make up those first roles, companies may save time today, but they will find it harder to develop their own talent in a few years. 

 SAP has a direct stake in this. Our customers and partners need people who can run the technology they buy, and many of those people will be young professionals starting out in markets where SAP is growing. 

 If young people cannot find a first job, they also miss the experience the digital economy will need from them later. 

 Why the UN General Assembly 

 Many different players shape whether young people find work. Governments shape education systems and labor markets, United Nations (UN) agencies and foundations run programs, and companies decide whom to hire. Each works on its own part, and young people often fall through the gaps in between. 

 UN General Assembly week is one of the few moments each year when these actors are in the same city at the same time. That is why SAP made youth skills and employment a focus there, alongside its long-standing partnership with UNICEF’s Generation Unlimited, whose Board SAP CEO Christian Klein chairs. 

 On a panel at the Generation Unlimited Global Leadership Council, Klein made the case that large AI investments should come with a plan for the people who will work with the technology, including young people looking for their first role. 

 Two ideas ran through the week. The first is that training only pays off when it connects to the next step. The Youth Livelihoods Alliance—which Generation Unlimited launched at SAP’s New York office with SAP, Accenture, and the Standard Chartered Foundation as founding partners—is built on that idea. It links the partners’ programs into one route from first skills to recognized credentials and a job, supported by Yoma, a digital platform where more than 1.3 million young people keep a verified record of what they have learned. 

 “The future of work cannot be built without young people,” said Rashmi Verma, chief inclusion and social impact officer at SAP. “While millions are developing valuable skills, too many still struggle to access meaningful employment. Closing that gap requires stronger collaboration between business, governments, and civil society. By connecting learning opportunities to real jobs, we can help ensure that young people are prepared not only to navigate an AI-powered economy, but to shape it.” 

 The second idea is that companies can contribute most through what they already do. Hiring from the programs they fund, buying from social enterprises, and lending their experts to social innovators can have a lasting effect—and companies can do all of it within their normal operations. 

 SAP works on this with the World Economic Forum, where it co-chairs the Corporate Leadership Council for Social Innovation, and with partners such as EY and Microsoft in Scaling AI for Good, a program that helps social innovators use AI in their work. 

 Next stop: Heidelberg 

 In Heidelberg, near SAP headquarters, young people will lead the discussion. From December 8-10, 2026, the UN Youth Office will host its first UN Youth Townhall. More than 1,000 young people will meet leaders from governments, the UN, academia, and business to develop recommendations on AI, future skills, and work. 

 SAP is a partner of the UN Youth Townhall and plans to support participation by young people from underrepresented backgrounds. 

 For companies, the question is how to turn what they hear in Heidelberg into action: opening routes into work, giving young people opportunities to gain experience, and involving them in decisions about how AI changes their jobs. 

 The conversation may begin at a town hall, but the response belongs in everyday business. 
 Subscribe to our newsletter to receive weekly news, stories, and highlights from the SAP News Center 

 Sign up here 

 *Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, 2026

items.title: Month-end close and AI agents: which steps would you actually hand over?
items.author: Farrukh_Gillani
items.text:
Hi everyone, 
 I've been reading a lot about Joule agents for finance (accruals, journal entries, clearing) and wanted to bring the discussion back to a normal month-end close. 
 In many S/4HANA companies the close looks like this: 
 order settlement every week, and again at month end 
 allocation percentages updated every quarter, then the allocation runs 
 AuC settlement 
 depreciation run and asset checks 
 GR/IR review and accruals 
 Timing matters. One failed step blocks the next, and the finance team spends a lot of time checking logs and chasing errors. 
 Some of this can already be scheduled with SAP Advanced Financial Closing. SAP is now adding AI agents for accruals and journal entries. But I haven't seen much yet for settlement, allocations or asset closing. 
 So my questions: 
 Which close steps would you trust an AI agent with today, and which only need good scheduling? 
 Where do you think AI adds the most value: running the steps, or the checks before and after (missing settlement rules, error logs, unusual variances)? 
 Is anyone already using AFC together with Joule agents? What worked for you? 
 My view as a finance person: the run itself is usually rule-based and fine with scheduling. The real time goes into the checks and corrections around it, and that's where I'd like AI to help, with the accountant still approving anything that posts. 
 Curious to hear how others see it.

items.title: The Cost of 'If It Ain't Broke, Don't Fix It': How the SAP BTP Certificate Migration (Note 3566727)
items.author: NaotoSakai
items.text:
Recently—and perhaps it is a bit improper to say so—I encountered a very fascinating phenomenon as an engineer, so I would like to share the background and a technical explanation of what happened. 
 At a certain customer’s site, a service  suddenly stopped working on October 15, 2026. We received a report that all client devices could no longer connect to SAP BTP. 
 Some of you might immediately recognize what happened just from that date: the root cause was related to the replacement of root certificates in the SAP BTP Cloud Foundry environment (migration to DigiCert Global Root G5), as explained in SAP Note 3566727. 
 1. The Edge Side (Arduino) Issue 
 This customer was operating an IoT system that sends sensor data from Arduino devices to a custom-developed service running on the SAP BTP Cloud Foundry environment. 
 Microcontrollers (such as Arduino), being embedded devices, do not have a general-purpose OS like a PC or smartphone. Therefore, root certificates for encrypted communication must be manually written inside the "sketch" (the program running on the Arduino) and flashed onto the microcontroller as firmware. 
 Note: When performing HTTPS communication on an Arduino (such as models equipped with a Wi-Fi module), the root certificate must be hardcoded into the program as a PEM-formatted string and loaded into the communication library. 
 More than five years had passed since this system went live. While hardware maintenance had been performed on components like the IoT sensors, the Arduino boards themselves and their internal sketches had been running almost completely maintenance-free. Consequently, the root certificates embedded in the sketches remained outdated (lacking G5 support), causing communication to be cut off the moment the switchover occurred on October 15. 
 The solution itself was straightforward: modify the Arduino sketch to embed the DigiCert Global Root G5 certificate and flash the updated firmware. (While easy to describe in writing, going on-site to connect via USB and re-flash the devices—or swapping them out with pre-flashed replacement Arduinos—must have been quite a heavy lift. ) 
 Just when we thought the issue was completely resolved... it turned out the story wasn't over yet. 
 2. The Application on Cloud Foundry 
 After completing the fixes on the Arduino side, we confirmed that a different error was now occurring on the Cloud Foundry application side: "Cannot connect to the bound SAP HANA Cloud database." 
 The customer’s application was built with Node. js (using the Node. js buildpack) and configured to connect to an SAP HANA Cloud database. Just to be sure, we checked the SAP HANA Cloud instance itself, which was up and running with no issues. 
 So, what was the problem? 
 Have you ever seen a warning banner in the BTP Cockpit's Cloud Foundry application list prompting you to migrate to a newer stack (such as cflinuxfs4 or cflinuxfs5 )? 

 As it turned out, the customer's Cloud Foundry application was running on the legacy cflinuxfs3 stack. Moreover, it had been running completely untouched for over five years without ever being redeployed or restaged. 
 Note: Even when containers are restarted during routine Cloud Foundry infrastructure maintenance, the previously built execution image (Droplet) continues to be reused unless the developer explicitly runs cf restage or redeploys the app. As a result, the OS stack and runtime versions remain frozen in time. 
 Here, cflinuxfs3 , cflinuxfs4 , and cflinuxfs5 refer to the Linux root filesystems (stacks) that serve as the underlying foundation for applications running on the Cloud Foundry PaaS. Specifically, they correspond to the base OS (Ubuntu) version of the container spun up when an app is deployed: 

 cflinuxfs3 : Ubuntu 18. 04 LTS (Bionic Beaver) / Deprecated & Retired 

 cflinuxfs4 : Ubuntu 22. 04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) 

 cflinuxfs5 : Ubuntu 24. 04 LTS (Noble Numbat) / Latest generation stack 
 On a standard Linux server, even Ubuntu 18. 04 LTS could have picked up the DigiCert G5 root certificate as long as packages like ca-certificates were kept up to date. However, that does not happen in an old Cloud Foundry container that has never been restaged. 
 Even more critically, this application was running on Node. js. Unless specific flags are configured, Node. js does not rely on the OS certificate store; instead, it references its own list of root certificates statically compiled into the Node. js binary itself. Because an outdated Node. js runtime from over five years ago was still running, the Node. js app acting as a client could not trust DigiCert Global Root G5, resulting in SSL/TLS handshake failures when trying to connect to SAP HANA Cloud. 
 Modernizing with a Boost from AI 
 After discussing how to proceed with the customer, we decided, "Let's treat this as a great opportunity to upgrade the underlying foundation as well," and proceeded to migrate the app to the latest stack ( cflinuxfs5 ) alongside the latest version of the Node. js runtime. 
 Because we were bridging a five-year gap, we ran into some compatibility issues caused by Node. js specification changes as well as npm library dependency errors. However, we were able to resolve them smoothly with the help of an LLM—specifically thanks to the AI chat feature in SAP Build Code . (In fact, knowing we could leverage this capability was part of what gave us the confidence to go ahead with the upgrade. ) 
 Key Takeaways 
 Fortunately, because this IoT system was an independent data-collection setup used to assist data analytics rather than a mission-critical core system, the incident did not result in major business disruption. Still, this experience offers several important lessons for operating systems in the cloud era: 

 "Stable Operation" Does Not Mean "Maintenance-Free" 
 In this case, outdated root certificates on both the edge side (Arduino) and the cloud side (legacy Cloud Foundry stack and runtime) caused a two-stage communication failure. Because OS-less IoT devices cannot automatically update their certificate stores, operational designs must account for certificate lifecycle transitions—such as introducing Over-The-Air (OTA) remote updates. However, since Arduino boards are inexpensive, preparing pre-flashed replacement units and swapping them out may actually be cheaper and more practical than building an OTA mechanism, especially considering hardware lifespan (while the microcontroller chip itself lasts a long time, the power supply circuitry on the board typically has a lifespan of around 5 to 10 years). 

 Even PaaS Requires Periodic "Refreshes" (Restaging) 
 Even in a PaaS environment like Cloud Foundry, leaving an application deployed and untouched for years causes its underlying stack and runtime (including Node. js's built-in certificate store) to go stale. Heeding the stack migration warnings in the BTP Cockpit and periodically restaging applications or updating buildpacks is the surest way to prevent sudden outages. 

 Lean Into New Technologies 
 Upgrading five-year-old Node. js code to a modern environment would normally be a tedious process involving extensive library compatibility research. By leveraging the AI chat capabilities in SAP Build Code, we got through it remarkably smoothly. Turning an incident response into an opportunity to modernize the entire system with the help of AI was a major win. 
 If you have applications on SAP BTP that have been "running happily" for years, it might be a good time to peek into your BTP Cockpit and check whether they are still sitting on an outdated stack or runtime. 

 Regards,

items.title: Dynamic Mileage Facet Visibility in SAPRAP-Based Travel Expense Applications Using a Virtual Element
items.author: _Samitha-2018_
items.text:
While working on the SAP Travel Expense application, I encountered a requirement to control the visibility of the Mileage section based on the selected travel mode. The section should be displayed only when an employee selects Car and remain hidden for other modes such as Train, Flight, or Bus. 
 Initially, I considered handling this through UI configuration. However, my investigation revealed that the standard application determines Mileage facet visibility through a virtual element in the SAP RAP consumption layer. 
 This led me to explore the underlying standard logic and identify a way to extend it without directly modifying the UI configuration. 
 In this article, I will explain the standard implementation, my technical investigation, and how an implicit enhancement can be used to achieve condition-based facet visibility.

items.title: Creating Sales Orders in SAP Through EDI – Understanding the Process
items.author: Sneka_E
items.text:
Introduction 
 In today's business environment, many companies exchange purchase orders and other business documents electronically rather than relying on manual communication. When customers and suppliers use different systems, transferring order information accurately and on time becomes important. This is where Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) plays a major role. 
 In SAP Sales and Distribution (SD), EDI helps automate the process of receiving customer purchase orders and creating sales orders without manually entering the order details. In this blog, I will share a business scenario I worked on, explain how the process flows from a customer's purchase requisition to sales order creation in SAP, and highlight some of the technical components and common errors involved. By the end, you will have a clearer understanding of how EDI supports day-to-day sales operations. 
 1. What is EDI? 
 EDI stands for Electronic Data Interchange. It is a method of exchanging business documents between two companies in a standard electronic format. 
 For example, when a customer sends a purchase order to a supplier, the order details can be transferred electronically to the supplier's SAP system instead of being entered manually by the sales team. 
 This helps reduce manual effort, avoid data-entry errors, and speed up order processing. 
 2. A Business Scenario – From Customer PR to SAP Sales Order 
 I had an opportunity to work on an EDI-based sales order integration where both the customer and our company were using SAP. What made this process interesting was that the sales order creation was not the first step. There was a business approval process before the actual purchase order was sent to our SAP system. 
 Let's understand the process with a simple example. 
 Imagine a customer wants to purchase a chemical product from our company. 
 Step 1: Customer creates a Purchase Requisition (PR) 
 The customer first creates a Purchase Requisition in their SAP system and sends it to the SNC (Supplier Network Collaboration) portal. The PR contains details such as the required product, quantity, and delivery requirements. 
 Step 2: PR review and approval 
 Our company receives the PR through the SNC portal. The relevant business team reviews the request and approves it. Once approved, a response is sent back to the customer's system. 
 Step 3: Customer creates a Purchase Order (PO) 
 After receiving the approval response, the customer creates the actual Purchase Order in their SAP system. This PO contains the agreed product and order details. 
 Step 4: PO is transferred through EDI 
 Instead of manually entering the customer's PO into our SAP system, the order information is exchanged electronically through EDI. The middleware or integration layer handles communication and message mapping before transferring the information to the receiving SAP system. 
 Step 5: SAP receives the inbound IDoc 
 The incoming PO information reaches our SAP system as an inbound IDoc. SAP processes the IDoc and performs the necessary validations, such as checking customer details, material numbers, quantities, and other relevant order information. 
 Step 6: Sales Order is created automatically 
 If all the required validations are successful, SAP automatically creates a sales order. The sales team does not need to enter the customer's PO details manually. This makes the order creation process faster and reduces the possibility of manual errors. 
 3. Important SAP Technical Components 
 A few SAP technical components are important in this integration: 
 Component Purpose 
 IDoc Intermediate Document used to exchange business data between SAP and external systems. 
 Message Type ORDERS identifies the type of business message being exchanged. 
 Basic Type ORDERS05 is commonly used for inbound purchase order processing. 
 Partner Profile WE20 defines communication settings for the business partner. 
 IDoc Monitoring WE02 / WE05 are used to monitor IDoc status and errors. 
 Reprocessing BD87 is used to reprocess eligible IDocs after correcting errors. 
 4. What Happens When an Error Occurs? 
 One important point I noticed while working with this type of integration is that successful EDI transmission does not always mean successful sales order creation. 
 For example, the customer may send an incorrect material number, or the required customer-material mapping may be missing in the supplier's SAP system. In such cases, the inbound IDoc may fail during processing, and the sales order will not be created. 
 When this happens, the support team needs to investigate the issue rather than assuming that the order has been successfully received. 
 The usual checks include: 
 - Checking the inbound IDoc status and error details in WE02 or WE05. 
 - Identifying whether the issue is related to master data, mapping, or order information. 
 - Correcting the underlying issue with the relevant business or technical team. 
 - Reprocessing the IDoc using BD87, where appropriate. 
 This is why IDoc monitoring is an important part of supporting EDI integrations. 
 5. Conclusion 
 EDI is more than just transferring a purchase order from one system to another. It connects the business processes of customers and suppliers and helps automate activities that would otherwise require manual effort. 
 Through this scenario, we looked at how a customer's purchase requisition is submitted through an SNC portal, reviewed and approved by the supplier, followed by the creation of a purchase order and its transfer to the supplier's SAP system through EDI. We also explored the role of inbound IDocs, important SAP transactions, and how errors can be identified and handled. 
 One key takeaway is that monitoring the inbound IDoc is just as important as setting up the integration. An order is not successfully created simply because the EDI message was transmitted; it must also be processed successfully in SAP. 
 I hope sharing this business scenario helps beginners and SAP SD consultants understand how EDI-based sales order creation works in a real business environment.

items.title: Testing AUTHORITY-CHECK in SAP RAP with ABAP Unit
items.author: Dadapeer
items.text:
Introduction 
 Authorization is an important part of every SAP application. In real-time business scenarios, different users have different permissions to create, update, and delete business data. 
 In the SAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP), authorization control helps developers decide whether a user is permitted to perform a particular operation on a business object. We can implement authorization checks in RAP using global authorization and instance authorization methods. In many implementations, the ABAP AUTHORITY-CHECK statement is used to verify whether the current user has the required authorization object and activity. 
 But implementing authorization logic is only one part of development. We also need to verify that the logic behaves correctly. 
 In this blog, I will demonstrate how I used ABAP Unit to test the AUTHORITY-CHECK in the GET_GLOBAL_AUTHORIZATIONS method in a RAP behavior implementation. I will also show how to execute the local handler method from a local test class and measure the code coverage using the ABAP Coverage tool in ADT. 
 The example uses a custom authorization object named Z_RAUTH_D1 with the authorization field ACTVT . 

 Business Scenario 
 Consider a Material Management application developed using RAP. 
 Different users should have different permissions: 

 Operation 
 Activity 
 Description 

 Create 
 01 
 Create material 

 Update 
 02 
 Change material 

 Display 
 03 
 Display material 

 Delete 
 06 
 Delete material 
 For this scenario, I created the authorization object Z_RAUTH_D1 and used the ACTVT field to control the permitted operations. 
 The requirement is to check whether the current user has the required activity before allowing the RAP operation. 

 Implementing Global Authorization in RAP 
 First, global authorization needs to be enabled in the behavior definition. 
 Example: authorization master ( global ) 
 Implementing AUTHORITY-CHECK 
 I implemented the authorization logic in the GET_GLOBAL_AUTHORIZATIONS method. METHOD get_global_authorizations.
 IF requested_authorizations-%create = if_abap_behv=>mk-on.
 AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'Z_RAUTH_D1' ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '01'.
 result-%create = COND #( WHEN sy-subrc = 0 THEN if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
 ELSE if_abap_behv=>auth-unauthorized ).
 ENDIF.

 IF requested_authorizations-%update = if_abap_behv=>mk-on.
 AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'Z_RAUTH_D1' ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '02'.
 result-%update = COND #( WHEN sy-subrc = 0 THEN if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
 ELSE if_abap_behv=>auth-unauthorized ).
 ENDIF.

 IF requested_authorizations-%delete = if_abap_behv=>mk-on.
 AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'Z_RAUTH_D1' ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '06'.
 result-%delete = COND #( WHEN sy-subrc = 0 THEN if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
 ELSE if_abap_behv=>auth-unauthorized ).
 ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD. 
 Understanding the implementation in GET_GLOBAL_AUTHORIZATIONS 
 First, the method checks which authorization operation has been requested. 
 It executes AUTHORITY-CHECK for the corresponding activity. 
 If sy-subrc = 0 , the authorization is successful. 
 Otherwise, the operation is marked as unauthorized. 
 The result is returned to the RAP framework. 
 Creating the local ABAP Unit test class: 
 First, declare the local test class as a friend of the behavior handler. 

 The test class definition: 
 CLASS ltc_te_material_V DEFINITION FINAL
FOR TESTING
DURATION SHORT
RISK LEVEL HARMLESS.

 lt_result_auth TYPE STRUCTURE FOR GLOBAL AUTHORIZATION RESULT zi_te_material_v,
 lt_reported_auth TYPE RESPONSE FOR REPORTED EARLY zi_te_material_v.

ENDCLASS. 
 The FRIENDS addition allows the test class to access the local handler class. 

 Creating the test object 
 In the SETUP method, create an instance of the local handler. METHOD setup.
 CREATE OBJECT obj FOR TESTING.
 environment->clear_doubles( ).

* go_env->clear_doubles( ).
 ENDMETHOD. 
 Writing the ABAP Unit test method 
 The following is the central part of my test implementation. 
 METHOD test_global_auth.
* lt_inventory_mock = VALUE #( (
* materialid = 2
* orderid = 5
* materialname = 'PEN'
* quantity = 5

* materialid = 2
* orderid = 5
* materialname = 'PEN'
* quantity = 5
* price = '20.00'
** ) ).
"Test CREATE authorization
 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%create = '01'.

 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING
 requested_authorizations = me->lt_imp_auth_key
 CHANGING

 reported = lt_reported_auth
 ).

 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).

 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(
 act = lt_result_auth-%create
 exp = '01' ).

 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%create = '00'.
 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING
 requested_authorizations = me->lt_imp_auth_key
 CHANGING
 result = lt_result_auth
 reported = lt_reported_auth
 ).
 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).

"Test UPDATE authorization
 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%update = '01'.
 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING
 requested_authorizations = me->lt_imp_auth_key
 CHANGING
 result = lt_result_auth
 reported = lt_reported_auth
 ).
 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).

 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(
 act = lt_result_auth-%update
 exp = '01' ).

 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%update = '00'.
 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING

 CHANGING
 result = lt_result_auth
 reported = lt_reported_auth
 ).
 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).
"Test DELETE authorization
 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%delete = '01'.
 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING

 CHANGING

 ).
 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).

 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(

 me->lt_imp_auth_key-%delete = '00'.
 obj->get_global_authorizations(
 EXPORTING
 requested_authorizations = me->lt_imp_auth_key
 CHANGING

 ).
 cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_not_initial( lt_result_auth ).
 ENDMETHOD. 
 code coverage 
 Screenshot 1 – Branch coverage 

 2 – Statement coverage 
 Conclusion: 
 In this practical example, I demonstrated how to test a RAP global authorization method using ABAP Unit. We implemented authorization checks using the AUTHORITY-CHECK statement and created a local test class to execute the behavior handler method. The key learning is that implementing authorization logic is not enough. We should also verify the allowed and unauthorized scenarios through automated tests. ABAP Unit helps us identify untested branches and improves the reliability and maintainability of RAP applications. 
 I hope this example helps developers who are working with authorization control and ABAP Unit testing in SAP RAP.

items.title: Maintaining Classification Codes in Core Data Management for Next Gen SAP Ariba Buying
items.author: DDINESH
items.text:
Introduction 
 Classification codes are fundamental to organizing procurement data in Next Gen SAP Ariba Buying. This guide explains what classification codes are, why they matter, and provides a step-by-step walkthrough for uploading and configuring them using Core Data Management (CDM). 
 What are Classification Codes? ( Help Link ) 
 Classification codes (also called commodity codes ) are standardized taxonomies used to categorize goods and services in a hierarchical structure. In SAP Ariba Buying, the commodity code domain determines which hierarchy and mappings are applied to purchase requests. 
 Supported Classification Standards 
 SAP Ariba Buying supports multiple commodity code domains: 

 Standard 
 Description 
 Common Use 

 UNSPSC 
 United Nations Standard Products and Services Code 
 Default domain; global multi-sector standard 

 eClass 
 European classification standard 
 Commonly used in EU for product data 

 ASCC 
 Services classification 
 Service procurement 

 Custom Domain 
 Organization-specific taxonomy 
 Internal custom classification standards 
 UNSPSC Hierarchy Structure (Default) 
 Segment (2-digit) → e.g., 43 - Information Technology 
 └─ Family (4-digit) → e.g., 4321 - Computer Equipment 
 └─ Class (6-digit) → e.g., 432115 - Computers 
 └─ Commodity (8-digit) → e.g., 43211503 - Notebook computers 

 Level 
 Example 
 Description 
 Parent Code 

 2-digit 
 15 
 Segment 
 All 

 4-digit 
 1510 
 Family 
 15 

 6-digit 
 151015 
 Class 
 1510 

 8-digit 
 15101502 
 Commodity 
 151015 
 Parent Code Rules: 
 8-digit code's parent = first 6 digits 
 6-digit code's parent = first 4 digits 
 4-digit code's parent = first 2 digits 
 2-digit code's parent = "All" 
 Why are Classification Codes Required? 
 The commodity code domain determines: 
 Which commodity code hierarchy is applied when buyers select codes 
 Product classification mappings for catalog items 
 Material group determination for ERP integration 
 General ledger account assignment for financial posting 

 Purpose 
 Benefit 

 Spend Visibility 
 Aggregate and analyze spending across similar categories 

 Catalog Organization 
 Structure catalog items logically for easy discovery 

 Approval Routing 
 Route requisitions to appropriate category managers 

 Supplier Management 
 Match suppliers to relevant product/service categories 

 Compliance & Reporting 
 Meet regulatory requirements for spend reporting 

 ERP Integration 
 Map to SAP S/4HANA material groups and GL accounts 

 Benchmarking 
 Compare spending against industry standards 
 Key Configuration Points - Critical for Success 
 This section addresses the most common configuration mistakes that cause classification codes to fail. Read this carefully before uploading any data. 
 Single Active Domain Rule ( Help Link ) 
 SAP Ariba Buying uses only one active commodity code domain for all new requests at any given time. 
 What this means: 
 You cannot have UNSPSC and eClass active simultaneously 
 All catalogs, mappings, and accounting defaults must use the same domain 
 Changing the domain affects how the system resolves commodity codes for ALL new transactions 
 Why Change the Domain AFTER Uploading Data? 
 This is the most misunderstood configuration step. 
 The dropdown values in Default Domain are loaded from the Product Classification Codes entity in CDM. Until you upload classification codes with your domain name, that domain will NOT appear in the dropdown list. 
 Simply put: 
 No upload → No domain in dropdown → Cannot select your domain 
 Upload first → Domain appears in dropdown → Can select your domain 
 The sequence matters because: 

 Step 
 What Happens 
 Why This Order 

 1. Upload classification codes 
 Data is loaded into CDM with your domain name (e.g., "custom") 
 Domain value now exists in the system and appears in dropdown 

 2. Upload classification code mappings 
 Mappings reference the same domain name 
 Mappings connect codes to material groups 

 3. THEN change the domain in Admin Center 
 Select your domain from dropdown (now visible) 
 System now uses your domain for lookups 
 What you'll see: 
 BEFORE uploading classification codes: 
 ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ Default Domain: [dropdown ▼] │ 
 │ • UNSPSC │ ← Only default option visible 
 │ (your domain NOT listed) │ 
 └─────────────────────────────────┘ 

 AFTER uploading classification codes with domain = "custom": 
 ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ Default Domain: [dropdown ▼] │ 
 │ • UNSPSC │ 
 │ • custom │ ← Your domain NOW appears! 
 └─────────────────────────────────┘ 
 Correct sequence: 
 ✅ Right Sequence: 
 Upload classification codes with domain = "custom" 
 → "custom" now appears in Default Domain dropdown 
 Upload classification code mappings with domain = "custom" 
 Open Default Configuration in Admin Center 
 Select "custom" from the dropdown (now visible) 
 Save 
 Consistent Domain Naming - The #1 Cause of Failures 
 The domain name must be IDENTICAL (including case) across ALL of these: 

 Entity/Location 
 Field Name 
 Example Value

 custom

 Problem

 Use custom everywhere 
 Case mismatch - mappings won't resolve 

 UNSPSC in codes, unspsc in mappings 
 Use unspsc everywhere 
 Case mismatch - mappings won't resolve 

 my-domain in codes, my_domain in catalog 
 Use identical spelling 
 Character mismatch - catalog items won't map 
 How to verify consistency: 
 Export data from Product Classification Code entity - note the exact domain value 
 Use that EXACT value (copy-paste) in all other entities and configurations 
 Version Field Consistency 
 The Version field must also match across entities: 

 If Classification Codes use 
 Then Mappings must use 
 And Catalog must use 

 Version = 0 
 From Version = 0

 From Version = 25

 Tip: For custom domains, use 0 as the version to keep it simple. 
 Parent Code Hierarchy - Required for Material Group Resolution (Optional) 
 If you don't set up parent codes correctly, the hierarchical fallback for material group determination won't work. 
 Example of correct parent setup:

 What happens without proper parents: 
 Buyer selects item with code 48101599 (not directly mapped) 
 System tries to find parent 481015 → not found (no parent defined) 
 System cannot traverse hierarchy 
 Falls back to default (*) mapping instead of more specific match 
 How to Upload Classification Codes ( Help Link ) 
 Data Preparation 
 Before uploading classification codes, download the sample template from Core Data Management (CDM) by clicking Download Sample on the Product Classification Code entity.

 Real Example: Filled Excel Template 
 Here's a complete example showing how to fill the Product Classification Code sheet for a custom domain:

 Key points in this example: 
 Domain is consistently custom (lowercase) for all rows 
 Version is consistently 0 for all rows 
 Parent codes create a proper hierarchy: All → IT → IT-HW → IT-HW-001 
 Root level "All" has no parent (this is correct) 
 General Instructions for File Preparation 
 Do not modify sheet names or field names 
 Enter values under the same column as field name 
 Do not leave blank lines 
 Do not merge multiple cells 
 Do not apply formulas 
 Do not change the order of sheets 
 Upload Procedure 
 Prerequisites 
 Configure required integration and assign necessary business roles, business catalogs, and user roles to manage data in the connected ERP system 
 Assign the user group "cap - Manager" which provides: 
 View-only access to the core data entities list and file upload logs 
 Upload access for all allowed entities 
 Download access for allowed 'common' entities 
 Maintain material groups in SAP Central Business Configuration before maintaining classification codes 
 Steps to Upload Classification Codes 
 Prepare Classification Data 
 Obtain commodity code hierarchy data from your domain provider 
 Populate the template following the format and example above 
 Verify: Domain name is identical in every row 
 Access Core Data Management 
 Open the Master Data File Upload tile on the SAP Fiori launchpad 
 Upload Product Classification Codes 
 Open the Product Classification Codes entity 
 Upload the commodity code hierarchy 
 Select Common as the business system ID in the Source System field 
 Review the uploaded information after completion 
 Access Default Configurations 
 Open the Default Configuration app in Global Settings of Administration Center 
 Update the Domain to the one you have uploaded now and Save it 
 Important: Only do this step AFTER uploading classification codes AND mappings 
 Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them 

 Mistake 
 Symptom 
 Solution 

 Changing domain before uploading data 
 Material group not determined 
 Upload all data first, then change domain 

 Case mismatch in domain names 
 Mappings don't resolve 
 Copy-paste domain name to ensure consistency 

 Missing parent codes 
 Hierarchical fallback doesn't work 
 Define parent for every code except root 

 Different versions across entities 
 Lookups fail 
 Use same version everywhere 

 Spaces in domain name 
 Parsing errors 
 Use hyphens or underscores instead 
 Verification Checklist 
 After uploading, verify these items: 
 [ ] Classification codes visible in Product Classification Code entity 
 [ ] Domain name is consistent (check a few records) 
 [ ] Version is consistent

items.title: 「動いているから触らない」の代償：SAP BTPの証明書移行（Note 3566727）で5年稼働のIoTシステムが止まった話
items.author: NaotoSakai
items.text:
最近（少し不謹慎と言えるかもしれませんが）エンジニアとして非常に興味深い現象に遭遇したため、 その経緯と技術的な解説を共有したいと思います。 
 とあるお客様で、 2026年10月15日から突然サービスが稼働しなくなるという事態が発生しました。 全てのクライアント端末からSAP BTPに接続ができなくなったとのことでした。 
 この日付からピンと来る方もいるかと思いますが、 原因は SAP Note 3566727 で解説されている、 SAP BTP Cloud Foundry環境のルート証明書の置き換え（DigiCert Global Root G5への移行）に関わる問題です。 
 1.エッジ側（Arduino）の問題 実はこのお客様は、 ArduinoからSAP BTP Cloud Foundry環境のお客様開発のサービスへセンサーデータを送信している、 いわゆるIoTシステムを運用されていました。 
 組み込み端末であるマイコン（Arduino）は一般的なPCやスマートフォンのようなOSを持たず、 通信暗号化のためのルート証明書も「スケッチ」（Arduino上で動作するプログラム）内に手動で記述し、 マイコンのファームウェアとして書き込む必要があります。 
 ※注記：Arduino（Wi-Fiモジュール搭載機など）でHTTPS通信を行う際は、 使用するルート証明書をPEM形式で「プログラム内に文字列としてハードコード」し、 通信用のライブラリに読み込ませて使用します。 
 このシステムは稼働開始から5年以上が経過しており、 IoTセンサーなどのハードウェア保守は行われていたものの、 Arduino本体および内部のスケッチはほぼノーメンテナンスで動作し続けていました。 そのため、 スケッチに組み込まれているルート証明書が古いまま（G5非対応のまま）になっており、 10月15日の切り替えタイミングで通信が遮断された、 というわけです。 
 解決策自体はシンプルで、 Arduinoのスケッチを修正し、 DigiCert Global Root G5の証明書を組み込んだプログラムを書き込めば完了です。 （文章で言うのは簡単ですが、 現地でUSBを繋いで書き込むか、 修正プログラム書き込み済みのArduinoと交換する作業は大変だったと思います。 ） 
 これで無事問題は解決……と思いきや、 実はまだ終わらなかったのです。 
 2. Cloud Foundry上のアプリケーション Arduino側の対応完了後、 今度はCloud Foundry上のアプリケーション側で別のエラーが発生していることが確認できました。 「バインドしているSAP HANA Cloudデータベースに接続できない」というエラーです。 
 お客様のアプリケーションはNode. js（Node. jsビルドパック）で構築されており、 そこからSAP HANA Cloudデータベースへ接続する構成でした。 念のため確認しましたが、 SAP HANA Cloudデータベース自体は正常に稼働しており、 問題はありません。 
 では、 何が問題だったのか？ 
 BTP CockpitでCloud Foundry上のアプリ一覧を表示したとき、 新しいスタック（cflinuxfs4 や cflinuxfs5 など）への移行を促す警告表示を見たことはないでしょうか？ 
 実はお客様のCloud Foundry上のアプリケーションは、 古い cflinuxfs3 で動作していました。 そしてこちらも5年以上ノーメンテナンスで、 一度も再デプロイ（再ステージング）されることなく動作し続けていたのです。 
 ※Cloud Foundryの基盤メンテナンスでコンテナが再起動されることはあっても、 開発者側で cf restage や再デプロイを行わない限り、 過去にビルドされた実行イメージ（Droplet）がそのまま使われ続けるため、 OSスタックやランタイムのバージョンは古いまま維持されます。 
 ここで登場する cflinuxfs3 や cflinuxfs4、 cflinuxfs5 というのは、 PaaS基盤であるCloud Foundryにおいて、 アプリケーションが動作する土台となるLinuxのルートファイルシステム（スタック）の名称です。 アプリをデプロイした際、 裏側で起動するコンテナのベースOS（Ubuntu）のバージョンを指しています。 
 ・cflinuxfs3：Ubuntu 18. 04 LTS (Bionic Beaver) ／ 非推奨・廃止済み ・cflinuxfs4：Ubuntu 22. 04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) ・cflinuxfs5：Ubuntu 24. 04 LTS (Noble Numbat) ／ 最新世代スタック 
 通常のLinuxサーバーであれば、 OSの ca-certificates パッケージなどを更新していればUbuntu 18. 04 LTSであってもDigiCert G5のルート証明書を取り込めます。 しかし、 再ステージングされていない古いCloud Foundryコンテナではそうはいきません。 
 さらに重要な点として、 今回のアプリは Node. js で動作していました。 Node. jsは（特別なオプションを指定しない限り）OSの証明書ストアではなく、 Node. jsバイナリ自体に静的に組み込まれた独自のルート証明書リストを参照します。 つまり、 5年以上前の古いNode. jsランタイムがそのまま使われていたため、 クライアントとなるNode. jsアプリ自身がDigiCert Global Root G5を信頼できず、 SAP HANA CloudへのSSL/TLS接続でエラーを起こしていたのです。 
 AIの力も借りてモダン化へ どう対応すべきかお客様と協議した結果、 「逆に良い機会なので基盤ごと更新しよう」ということになり、 最新のスタック（cflinuxfs5）環境への移行と、 最新版のNode. jsランタイムへのバージョンアップを実施しました。 
 5年分のギャップがあるため、 一部Node. jsの仕様変更による互換性問題やNPMライブラリの依存関係エラーも発生しましたが、 LLMの力も借りてスムーズに解消することができました。 まさに SAP Build CodeのAIチャット機能 のおかげです。（これが活用できるという目論見があったため更新するという判断になったとも言えます。） 

 まとめ お客様にとっても、 このIoTシステムは基幹業務に直結するものではなく、 データ分析の一助となる独立したデータ収集システムであったため、 結果として大きな業務影響には至りませんでした。 しかし、 今回の事象からはクラウド時代のシステム運用における重要な教訓が得られました。 

 ■ 「安定稼働＝メンテナンスフリー」ではない 今回のように、 エッジ側（Arduino）とクラウド側（Cloud Foundryの古いスタック・ランタイム）の双方でルート証明書が古くなっていたことで、 二重の通信エラーが発生しました。 特にOSを持たないIoTデバイスは証明書の自動更新が効かないため、 証明書の世代交代を見据えた運用設計（OTAによる遠隔更新の導入など）が欠かせません。 但し、 Arduinoであれば安価であるためOTA機構導入より、 耐用年数も考慮し交換用の機器を用意して交換のほうが安い＆良いかもしれません。 チップ自体耐用年数的に問題ないものの、基盤の 電源周りの耐用年数は5年〜10年ではないか？とも聞きますし。 

 ■ PaaSでも定期的な「リフレッシュ（再ステージング）」が必要 Cloud FoundryのようなPaaS環境であっても、 何年もデプロイしっぱなしにしていると基盤（スタック）やランタイム（Node. js内蔵の証明書ストア）が陳腐化します。 BTP Cockpitのスタック移行警告を放置せず、 定期的に再ステージングやビルドパックの更新を行うことが、 突然のトラブルを防ぐ一番の近道です。 
 ■ テクノロジーの活用を また、 5年前のNode. jsコードを最新環境へ引き上げる作業は、 本来であればライブラリ互換性の調査などで骨が折れるものですが、 SAP Build CodeのAIチャット機能を活用することで非常にスムーズに乗り切ることができました。 トラブル対応を単なる「復旧」で終わらせず、 AIの力を借りてシステム全体をモダン化できたのは大きな収穫でした。 
 ぜひ皆様も、 長年「元気に動き続けている」BTP上のアプリケーションが古いスタックやランタイムのままになっていないか、 一度BTP Cockpitを覗いてみてはいかがでしょうか。

items.title: Promoting Agents Across Joule Studio’s Three-Tier Environments Through Git Workflows
items.author: LeileiZhou
items.text:
Leilei Zhou is a Product Manager for Joule Studio, focusing on Agent lifecycle management. 
 1. Introduction: 
 From Development to Production An AI agent is not simply production-ready because its code runs successfully in a developer’s environment. Its prompts, tools, model configuration, dependencies, and security settings must be validated consistently before reaching end users. In Joule Studio, users with developer role can create Agent, while Git integration provides a structured way to review changes and automate promotion workflows. With combination of Joule Studio and Git workflows, administrators can move Agents across three environments—Development, Test/Staging, and Production. 
 This article explains how to implement this promotion process for Agents in Joule Studio through Git workflows. 

 2. Three-Tier Environment and Promotion Model 
 A three-tier environment—Development, Test, and Production—is a common pattern in enterprise IT. Joule Studio can follow this established model to separate Agent development, validation, and operation across independent tenants. Each tenant includes Joule Work and Joule Studio, SAP Cloud Identity, and connections to SAP and non-SAP applications. 

 An Agent is initially created and developed in the Development Tenant. 
 After the changes are ready for testing, the Agent is promoted to the Test Tenant, where it can be validated in a controlled environment. 

 Once the required checks are completed, an administrator can promote the Agent to the Production Tenant. 
 Git workflows coordinate this promotion process by providing a structured way to review changes, execute validation steps, and manage the transition between tenants. Joule Studio remains the platform where users create and manage Agents. 

 3. End-to-End Agent Promotion Process 
 3.1 Prepare the Agent in Development 
 The promotion process starts in the Development Tenant. In Joule Studio, users can create and prepare an Agent through the following steps: 
 Enter an intent and create the Agent : Enter the intended business outcome and follow the conversation in the chat box to complete the Agent creation process. 
 Deploy and test the Agent in the Sandbox :Deploy the Agent to the Sandbox environment and try it with representative scenarios. Use this step to verify the Agent’s basic behavior before sharing it with other environments. 
 Connect the Solution to a Git Repository : Connect the Solution to a Git repository and push the Solution to the repository. This makes the Solution available for the Git-based review and promotion workflow. 
 3.2 Customize the Git workflows for the Test and Production Tenant 
 After the Solution is pushed to the Git repository, the deployment workflow files used for promotion are generated automatically in the repository. This section uses GitHub as an example of a Git provider. The same principles can be applied to other supported Git providers with the corresponding configuration. The following steps show how to customize the workflow for the Test Tenant. 
 Configure the Test Tenant in SAP Cloud Identity Services 
 Sign in to SAP Cloud Identity Services (SCI) for the Test Tenant with administrator permissions. Follow Step 1 of the GitHub setup guide to create and configure an application for the Test Tenant. 
 Configure GitHub organization-level secrets 
 Sign in to GitHub with GitHub organization administrator permissions. Follow Step 2 of the GitHub setup guide to configure the variables and secrets required by the Test Tenant. 
 To distinguish the Test Tenant from other environments, use environment-specific names such as: TEST_SCI_TENANT_URL

TEST_SCI_CLIENT_ID

TEST_JOULE_STUDIO_URL

TEST_SCI_CLIENT_SECRET 
 Create a Test deployment workflow 
 Copy the generated sample workflow file: .github/workflows/deploy.yml 
 and save the copy as: . github/workflows/deploy-to-test.yml 
 Update the Test deployment workflow 
 Open deploy-to-test.yml and make the following changes: 
 1. Change the workflow name from 'Deploy to Joule Studio' to 'Deploy to Joule Studio Test Tenant' 
 2. Replace the default environment variable and secret names wherever they are used: SCI_TENANT_URL → TEST_SCI_TENANT_URL
SCI_CLIENT_ID → TEST_SCI_CLIENT_ID
JOULE_STUDIO_URL → TEST_JOULE_STUDIO_URL
SCI_CLIENT_SECRET → TEST_SCI_CLIENT_SECRET 
 Run the Test Tenant deployment workflow 
 Open the Actions tab in the GitHub repository. You should see the new workflow named ‘Deploy to Joule Studio Test Tenant’ . This workflow can now be used to deploy the Solution to the Test Tenant. 
 The same approach can be used to configure the Production Tenant, using its own SCI application, environment-specific secrets, and production deployment workflow. 
 3.3 Deploy and Validate the Agent in the Test Tenant 
 After the Test Tenant workflow has been configured, the Solution can be deployed to the Test Tenant for validation. 
 Push changes to Git Repository: Commit the latest Agent changes and push them to Git repository. 
 Run the Test tenant deployment workflow: Open the Actions tab in GitHub and select ‘Deploy to Joule Studio Test Tenant’. 
 Monitor the deployment: Review the workflow run and its logs to confirm that the Solution is packaged and deployed successfully. The workflow uses the Test Tenant-specific URLs, client ID, and client secret configured in the previous step. 
 Validate the Agent in Test Tenant: After deployment, open the Agent in the Test Tenant and test it with representative business scenarios. Verify the Agent’s responses, tool calls, integrations, and other expected behaviors. 
 Once the required tests and validations are complete, the Solution is ready for the next stage of the promotion process: approval and deployment to the Production Tenant. 
 3.4 Promote the Agent to the Production Tenant 
 Before deploying the Solution to the Production Tenant, create a release in Joule Studio and complete required approval process. A release represents the version of the Solution that is ready to be promoted to Production. For detailed instructions, see Create a release with the Web UI . 
 Create a release in Joule Studio: Open the Solution in Joule Studio and create a release using the Web UI. After the release is created, identify the corresponding release tag. 
 Open the Production deployment workflow in GitHub : In the GitHub repository, go to Actions and select Deploy to Joule Studio Production Tenant. 
 Select the release tag : Start the workflow and select the release tag that corresponds to the release created in Joule Studio. This ensures that the intended Solution version is deployed to the Production Tenant. 
 Run and monitor the deployment: Start the workflow and monitor its execution logs. After the workflow completes successfully, verify that the Agent is available and operates as expected in the Production Tenant. 

 5. Conclusions 
 A reliable Agent promotion process depends on clear separation between the Development, Test, and Production Tenants. Joule Studio provides the environment for creating and managing Agent Solutions and releases, while Git workflows support collaboration, validation, and controlled deployment across tenants. 
 When implementing this process: 
 - Keep tenant-specific configuration and credentials separate. 
 - Use appropriate permissions for Joule Studio and GitHub. 
 - Validate the Solution in the Test Tenant before Production deployment. 
 - Align the Joule Studio release with the corresponding Git release tag. 
 - Retain deployment logs and approval records for traceability. 
 This approach provides a structured path from Agent creation to Production deployment.

items.title: Conflicting Users in Identity Provisioning: It's About Matching, Not Fighting
items.author: ivelinakiryakov
items.text:
Imagine you booked a hotel room online and arrive to check in. The receptionist tries to create a new guest record but receives an error: "Guest already exists." 
 It turns out you're already in the hotel's system from a previous stay. The reservation is valid, but the hotel doesn't need a second version of you. Instead, it needs to find your existing record and update the reservation. 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Provisioning (IPS) faces similar situations when provisioning users or groups that already exist in a target system. In this blog post, we'll explore what conflicts are, how IPS resolves them, common conflict-resolution scenarios and a few takeaways for troubleshooting and configuration. 

 What Is a Conflicting User? 

 A conflicting user is an incoming user whose creation fails because the value of an attribute that must be unique, such as a username or email address, already exists in the target system. 
 Consider this example: 
 1. You provision the user Joe Dow from Microsoft Entra ID to the Identity Directory (IDDS) target system with userName=JoeDow . As a result, the user is created. 

 2. You then provision a user from SAP SuccessFactors to the target system where a user with the same userName=JoeDow exists. 

 3. The target rejects the second creation attempt because that username already exists. Instead, it updates the user. 

 The incoming SAP SuccessFactors user is the conflicting user . IPS can attempt to resolve the conflict by identifying and updating the existing JoeDow. 
 Conflicts are not limited to multiple sources. They can also involve manually created users in the target system or different users within the same source system. 
 Note : A conflicting group follows the same principle. Its creation is rejected because an existing group already has a value, or combination of values, that must be unique. 
 The relevant attributes depend on the target connector and group type. For Identity Directory, the default for idds.group.unique.attribute is: ['urn:sap:cloud:scim:schemas:extension:custom:2.0:Group']['name'] 
 Application-specific groups can require additional matching attributes. Check the relevant connector documentation before configuring their conflict resolution. 

 How Conflict Resolution Works 

 Conflict resolution is configured on the target system. For Identity Directory, two properties are particularly important: 
 idds.user.automatic.conflict.resolution - Determines whether IPS should automatically attempt to resolve user creation conflicts. Default: true. 
 idds.user.unique.attribute - Defines the matching attribute (or combination of attributes) that IPS uses to locate an existing user after a creation conflict occurs. Default: userName. Other supported configurations include an email address or a combination of attributes. For example, userName,emails[0].value requires an existing user to match both values. 
 Both properties complement each other. One controls whether IPS attempts automatic conflict resolution. The other controls how IPS identifies the existing user. Automatic user conflict resolution is enabled when idds.user.automatic.conflict.resolution is true or is not configured. This property controls user conflicts, not group conflicts. For more information, see List of Properties . 
 The attribute that causes the conflict and the attribute used to resolve it are not necessarily the same . For example, the user creation may fail because an email address already exists and must be unique, while IPS searches for the existing user using userName matching attribute. 

 Three Practical Scenarios 

 The following scenarios assume idds.user.unique.attribute=userName and valid incoming user data. They compare the outcomes when idds.user.automatic.conflict.resolution is set to true or false. 

 Scenarios Automatic resolution enabled Automatic resolution disabled 

 A. JoeDow already exists. The creation of the incoming user conflicts with the existing JoeDow account. 
 IPS searches for userName=JoeDow, identifies the existing user, and attempts to update it. 
 IPS does not perform a conflict-resolution search. Provisioning fails and the existing JoeDow account is not updated. 

 B. JaneS is a new user. Neither her userName nor any other unique attribute conflicts with an existing account. IPS creates JaneS normally. IPS creates JaneS normally. There is no conflict to resolve. 

 C. JaneS has an email conflict. Her email address already belongs to an existing user with a different userName, and email uniqueness is enforced. IPS searches for userName=JaneS. No matching user is found, so conflict resolution fails. 
 IPS does not perform a conflict-resolution search. Provisioning fails after the creation conflict occurs. 

 If you set idds.user.automatic.conflict.resolution=false , scenarios A and C fail because user creation encounters a uniqueness conflict. IPS does not attempt to locate an existing user. 

 Scenario B remains unchanged because no conflict exists in the first place. 

 Key Takeaways 

 A conflicting user or group is an incoming identity whose creation encounters a uniqueness conflict with an existing target identity. 
 A new identity without a conflict can be created normally. 
 Conflict-resolution properties define how IPS searches for the existing identity. 
 The conflicting attribute can differ from the configured matching attribute. 
 After a creation conflict, if the search cannot identify the existing identity, provisioning fails. 
 Connector versions, group types, and configuration affect the matching behavior. 

 Handling conflicts correctly means knowing when to create a new identity, when to update an existing one, and when further investigation is needed. 
 Or, to put it another way, before provisioning an identity to a target system, IPS asks one simple question: 
 "Have we met before?"

items.title: SAP SPM Incentive Management - Data Integration - White Paper - Performance Tuning
items.author: Chris_Hovan62
items.text:
Performance testing, also known as load testing or performance tuning, must be conducted on every project. Performance testing is often incorrectly used synonymously with stress testing, but this is not an accurate statement. 
 Performance testing is conducted to ensure that the system runs optimally under normal data loads (expected volumes) with a reasonable margin of variability (+/- 5 to 10%). Load testing is a subset of performance testing focusing on the system’s ability to scale over time given normal increases in the amount of data. Stress testing, also a subset of performance testing, involves overloading a performance-tuned system to evaluate how well it performs under extreme conditions. 
 In Incentive Management, performance testing is done to ensure the datafiles load into the system successfully, the calculation pipelines execute successfully by the system, datafiles are successfully extracted from the system, and reports are successfully generated by the system, and each of those steps are running as well as possible. 
 This document will examine two main areas: data gathering and testing approach. Enough time must be spent on both areas to ensure that the testing is at the proper depth (data gathering) and breadth (testing approach).
